beats.text: He knocked out the Nazis' favorite boxer in two minutes and four seconds. Then his own government chased him for a debt he could never pay.

overlays.hook: He beat the Nazis' champion in 124 seconds. *Then America came for everything.*

beats.text: On a June night in 1938, seventy thousand people packed Yankee Stadium. Millions more were listening on the radio, in America and in Germany.
It took him two minutes and four seconds to win.
He held the heavyweight title for almost twelve years. He gave his prize money to the war effort. And then the government sent him the bill.
It is one of the strangest stories in American sport: the champion his country celebrated, and then would not let go of.
His name was Joe Louis. This is his story.
Joseph Louis Barrow was born on May 13th, 1914, in Chambers County, Alabama.
He was the seventh of eight children. His parents were sharecroppers, and both were the children of people who had been enslaved.
When Joe was two, his father was committed to a mental hospital. Joe would hardly know him.
In 1926, like millions of Black families in the Great Migration, they moved north, to Detroit.
There, Joe found a boxing gym. As an amateur, he won fifty of his fifty-four fights, forty-three by knockout.
In 1934 he won the national amateur light heavyweight title. That summer, he turned professional.
His first pro fight was on July 4th, 1934. He won in the first round.
His managers were two Black businessmen, John Roxborough and Julian Black.
They hired a trainer, the former fighter Jack Blackburn. He taught Joe to stay calm, set up his punches, and finish fights.
They knew what had happened to the last Black heavyweight champion, Jack Johnson. He had enraged white America, and for years after him, Black fighters were kept away from the title.

visual.title: After Jack Johnson
visual.sub: the title was kept from Black fighters

beats.text: When Johnson won the title in 1908, white promoters started hunting for a Great White Hope to take it back from him. Newspapers mocked him for years.
So they gave Joe rules. Never be photographed with a white woman. Never gloat over a beaten opponent. Keep a straight face.

visual.title: The rules
visual.sub: never gloat, keep a straight face

beats.text: He followed them. And he kept winning. In 1935, he beat the former champion Primo Carnera.
The press called him the Brown Bomber.
Then, in June 1936, he met the German former champion Max Schmeling at Yankee Stadium.
Louis was the favorite. But in the twelfth round, Schmeling knocked him out.
It was the first loss of his professional career.
In Germany, the Nazi regime made Schmeling a national hero.
Louis went back to work. A year later, on June 22nd, 1937, he fought the champion, James Braddock, in Chicago.
Braddock knocked him down in the first round.
Louis got up, and wore him down.
In the eighth round, he knocked Braddock out.
He was the heavyweight champion of the world. The first Black heavyweight champion in twenty-two years.

visual.caption: Louis declared the winner over Braddock, 1937

beats.text: But one loss still stood on his record.
The rematch with Schmeling was set for June 22nd, 1938, at Yankee Stadium.
By then it was more than a boxing match. Many Americans saw it as a contest between their country and Nazi Germany.
President Roosevelt reportedly told Louis: Joe, we need muscles like yours to beat Germany.

visual.quote: Joe, we need muscles like yours to beat Germany.
visual.by: President Roosevelt to Joe Louis, as reported

beats.text: Seventy thousand people came. Radio carried the fight around the world, including to Germany.
Louis came out punching, and he never stopped.
Schmeling went down. His corner threw in the towel.
It was over in two minutes and four seconds.
In Harlem, people poured into the streets and celebrated through the night.
Black Americans, and much of white America too, had a hero.
The next morning, the champion read about himself in the paper.

visual.caption: Louis reading the New York Daily News, 23 June 1938

beats.text: Over the next years, he fought almost anyone who would get in the ring with him.

visual.caption: Louis with a medal from The Ring, 1939

beats.text: Between 1939 and 1941, he defended the title thirteen times. Reporters called his opponents the Bum of the Month Club.
In 1941, the young Billy Conn was ahead on the scorecards. Louis knocked him out in the thirteenth round.
He was now one of the most famous men in America, Black or white. Children in every city knew his name.
In all, he would defend the title twenty-five times, and hold it for almost twelve years. Both are still heavyweight records.
Then came Pearl Harbor.
In January 1942, Louis fought Buddy Baer, and gave his purse to the Navy Relief Society.
Two months later, he fought Abe Simon, and gave that purse to the Army Relief Fund.
That same year, he joined the Army, an army that still kept Black and white soldiers apart.
He never saw combat. Instead he boxed in almost a hundred exhibitions for the troops, and toured camps and hospitals.

visual.caption: Louis signing autographs at a military hospital, about 1945

beats.text: The government put him on its posters.
But there was a problem with the money he gave away.
The tax collectors counted those charity purses as his income. He owed tax on money he never kept.

visual.title: Taxed
visual.sub: on the money he gave away

beats.text: He had given away the money. He still had to pay the tax on it, and the interest on the tax.
And in those years, the top income tax rates reached ninety percent. The more he earned, the more he owed.
On March 1st, 1949, Joe Louis retired, still the champion.
By 1950, the government said he owed more than half a million dollars. With interest and penalties, it kept growing, past one million.
So, at thirty-six, he came back.
On September 27th, 1950, he lost a fifteen-round decision to the new champion, Ezzard Charles.
He kept fighting.
In January 1951, he beat Freddie Beshore. He won his next fights too. For a moment, it looked like the old champion was back.
On October 26th, 1951, he met a young Rocky Marciano at Madison Square Garden.
In the eighth round, Marciano knocked him through the ropes.
Joe Louis never boxed again.
The debt did not go away. He took whatever work he could find.
He became a professional wrestler, then a wrestling referee.
Later he worked in Las Vegas, as a greeter at Caesars Palace, shaking hands with tourists.
In 1954, he was voted into the boxing Hall of Fame. But a plaque could not pay the tax bill.
He struggled with drugs and with his mental health.
One old opponent helped him. Max Schmeling, the man he had beaten in 1938, became his friend.
On April 12th, 1981, Joe Louis watched a heavyweight title fight in Las Vegas. Hours later, his heart failed. He was 66.
He had not served enough to be buried at Arlington National Cemetery by the usual rules. President Reagan waived them.
He was buried there with full military honors. Max Schmeling helped pay for the funeral, and was a pallbearer.
In 1982, Congress awarded him its Gold Medal.
Detroit, the city where he learned to box, had already named its new hockey arena for him: the Joe Louis Arena, opened in 1979.
He beat the Nazis' champion. He gave his purses to his country.
And his country taxed him for it, for the rest of his life.
That was Joe Louis. Subscribe for more.
